title: The Independent Public Advocate: scope, limits and what needs fixing
label: 13 October 2026 · IPA evidence session
summary: Cindy Butts, the first Independent Public Advocate (IPA) for England and Wales, told the Committee how her role works in practice, described urgent gaps in staffing, resourcing and legal access, explained limits on her powers when ‘stood down’ by the Secretary of State, and argued for a national body to track and enforce implementation of inquiry recommendations. She supports stronger transparency around decisions to hold inquiries and better coordination between the IPA and other accountability reforms.

speakers.label: Cindy Butts
speakers.name: Cindy Butts
speakers.role: Independent Public Advocate for England and Wales

glossary.definition: A statutory official who advocates for victims, survivors and bereaved people after major incidents and highlights systemic failings to Government.
A legal fact-finding hearing, led by a coroner, into the cause and circumstances of a death.
A formal government-led investigation with legal powers to gather evidence; a statutory inquiry follows rules set out in law.
A formal status in an inquiry giving rights to access evidence and participate in hearings.
A legal or policy obligation for public bodies to be open and honest about failings and share relevant information.
A bill referenced in the session that includes measures on official accountability, including a duty of candour.

chapters.title: What the IPA actually does
chapters.takeaway: The IPA is meant to be an independent, visible advocate for victims, helping them access support and navigate inquests and inquiries while flagging systemic failings to Ministers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Cindy, you've been the first IPA for almost a year. In plain terms, what have you been doing?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Four days after starting I was deployed to the Heaton Park synagogue attack. My job is to be an independent, visible advocate for victims, survivors and bereaved people: check they have support, help them navigate inquests, reviews and inquiries, make sure they can play a meaningful role, and report systemic gaps to Ministers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So you signpost services, press service providers, and spot system-wide problems for Government?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Yes. I'm not a service provider — I hold others to account and push for systemic learning where victims' needs are not being met.

chapters.title: Independence, structure and resourcing
chapters.takeaway: The IPA is independent in intent, but the office is tiny, relies on MOJ support, is only two days a week on paper, and needs more staff and secure independence to do the job well.

turns.speaker: John Lamont
turns.text: You're deployed only for 'major incidents' as defined by the Secretary of State. Does that limit your help?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Partly. I support deployed cases but also listen to legacy campaigners. The law's limits matter, but listening to those outside formal deployment tells us about system failings.

turns.speaker: Sarah Russell
turns.text: You work officially two days a week and have three staff; is that enough?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: No. I go full-time when deployed, but the part-time design cuts out many candidates and undermines readiness. We lack a separate office, own finance staff and scale-up capacity. I’ve put in a business case for more resources.

turns.speaker: Sarah Russell
turns.text: And the Children's Commissioner has 28 staff — that comparison matters?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Yes. More staff would let us dig into systemic policy issues and be resilient. Right now, the civil service sometimes holds the pen, which weakens perceived independence.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You rely on MOJ systems; that bureaucratic dependency slows you when needs are immediate?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Exactly. The bureaucracy and approvals slow urgent action, which is damaging in trauma situations.

chapters.title: Standing up, standing down and accountability
chapters.takeaway: The Secretary of State decides deployments and standing-down; the IPA can advise and report to Parliament, but there’s no independent appeal—more transparency and a clearer process are needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If the Secretary of State wants you stood down but you disagree, can you appeal?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Statutory guidance says the Secretary of State decides in consultation with me. There's no higher appeal, but I can report to Parliament and produce discretionary reports. What’s missing is a transparent process where reasons for standing up or down are public.

turns.speaker: Charlotte Cane
turns.text: You said people remain affected long after stand-down. How should that be handled?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: We need hybrid thinking: standing down shouldn't cut survivors off. Needs can appear years later; someone ought to pick up long-term support and follow-up on gaps identified at the time.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You plan a roundtable in November to clarify the IPA's role in inquiries?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Yes — with academics, practitioners and people with lived experience to work out how the IPA should participate in statutory and non‑statutory inquiries and what status is appropriate.

chapters.title: Inquiries, legal status and practical limits
chapters.takeaway: The IPA can be a core participant in inquests automatically but not automatically in inquiries; core participant status brings heavy document work and may need more staff and careful decisions about the IPA's role.

turns.speaker: Charlotte Cane
turns.text: Was the IPA involved in the decision to hold a public inquiry into Heaton Park?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: That decision followed disclosures to the coroner and the Chief Coroner's judgment; my counsel and I were involved in disclosure and made submissions about pros and cons, including closed evidence and absence of juries in inquiries.

turns.speaker: Charlotte Cane
turns.text: Will you automatically be a core participant in that inquiry?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: No. The law makes me an interested person in inquests, but not automatically a core participant in inquiries. Core participant status means handling huge volumes of disclosure and effectively servicing the inquiry, which I can only do with more staff. I'm still exploring the right status.

turns.speaker: John Lamont
turns.text: How do you advise families which route—coroner, inquiry, review—best suits their needs?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: I help them clarify what questions they need answered, then explain the pros and cons of each forum. Victims are not a single voice; my job is to represent that range and push for coherent views where possible.

chapters.title: Gaps in support, legal aid and follow-up on recommendations
chapters.takeaway: There are practical gaps: organisations like a synagogue can't access legal aid easily, carers lack benefits support after attacks, and inquiry recommendations too often sit unimplemented — so Cindy supports a separate national oversight mechanism.

turns.speaker: Charlotte Cane
turns.text: What gaps did you spot at Heaton Park?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: People felt overwhelmed by agencies. The synagogue, as an interested party, couldn't access legal aid because it's an organisation. There is also no consistent support route for people who suddenly become carers after an attack.

turns.speaker: Sam Carling
turns.text: You favour a national oversight mechanism (NOM) to track inquiry recommendations. Why a separate body?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Reports often cost a lot but recommendations aren't implemented; families end up policing progress. A statutory, independent body with expertise and a single accountable lead would keep recommendations live and drive change.

turns.speaker: Sam Carling
turns.text: Should the IPA do that NOM role?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: No. That would dilute the IPA's advocacy role. We should work closely with any NOM and feed in victims' experiences, but the oversight job needs dedicated capacity and independence.

turns.speaker: Peter Lamb
turns.text: How should Government improve implementation of recommendations?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Be clearer, faster and more transparent: publish which recommendations are accepted or rejected with reasons, set realistic timescales, and provide a public tracker with accountability rather than letting things languish.

chapters.title: Wider legal and devolution issues
chapters.takeaway: Cindy supports the Hillsborough law and duty of candour but worries the IPA wasn't linked into the Public Office (Accountability) Bill; she will expand coverage understanding differences in Wales and work with Scottish counterparts.

turns.speaker: Richard Baker
turns.text: You're the IPA for England and Wales; how will you engage with devolved systems?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: I need to understand Welsh structures and will recruit advocates who know Wales. I will visit Scotland and can work with Scottish bodies, but my statutory remit is England and Wales.

turns.speaker: Luke Taylor
turns.text: How important is Hillsborough law in changing defensive institutional cultures?

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Very important: it pushes truth-telling and legal parity between families and the state. But the law alone won't change culture; leadership and values matter. I'm concerned the IPA isn't mentioned in the Public Office (Accountability) Bill — that should be fixed so duty of candour and the IPA work together.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We will consider writing to the Bill Minister about that omission.

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Please do. There's cross-party interest already; aligning the Victims Act that created my role with accountability reforms would strengthen both.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Cindy — for your candour and for taking a difficult, under‑resourced role.

turns.speaker: Cindy Butts
turns.text: Thank you. I will report back on the roundtable and keep working to strengthen victims' voices and system learning.
